origin.fact: A fancy goldfish variety credited to China and Japan; its Japanese name is Chinshurin.
Selectively bred in China in the 20th century, then became popular in Japan.
Care sheet lists China as the origin.
Shop page gives China as the origin.

looks.fact: Round, almost spherical body often compared to a golf ball, with thick domed scales that look like pearls.
Doubled fins like a fantail. Fins can be long or short.
Breed standard: body depth over two-thirds of body length, domed scales, a single dorsal fin, paired other fins, and a divided, forked tail held above horizontal.
A good fish is bright and alert, with strong colour that reaches into the fins. Colours include metallic, orange, calico and solid black.
Raised scales feel hard and look white like pearls. Sold in metallic, semi-metallic and non-metallic scale types.
Colours sold in Vietnam include orange, red, white, black, brown, blue, purple and calico (ngũ hoa). Fins are short and the tail is forked.
Young fish look much like ordinary goldfish. The round body and clear pearl scales only show as they grow, so small fish are hard to judge.

lines.fact: Three head forms: no head growth, an oranda-like wen, or two large bubble-like domes (High-head Pearlscale, Crown Pearlscale or Hamanishiki).
The Crown pearlscale (Hamanishiki) has one or two lumps on its head and can grow larger than 15 cm.

keeping.fact: A coldwater fish that copes with cool water better than heat. It struggles in very hot places.
Tank of at least 60 L for one fish, plus about 30 L for each extra fish. Can also live in an outdoor pond.
Recommends a tank of at least 30 US gal (about 114 L). Use gentle filtration, such as a spray bar or lily pipe, because it swims poorly.
Keep it above 13 °C (55 °F) because it is sensitive to cold. Avoid sudden pH swings.
Feed sparingly because its compact body crowds the organs. Overfeeding causes problems.
Main food is good goldfish pellets, soaked before feeding. Add chopped boiled vegetables to prevent constipation. Give live or frozen food only now and then.
Feed twice a day, only what is eaten in 2 minutes. Add frozen foods and plant matter.
Possible tankmates are hardy coolwater fish such as zebra or pearl danios. Keep it away from fin nippers and fast or aggressive fish. Goldfish may eat shrimp.
Change 10–15% of the water each week.

breeding.fact: Can spawn in home tanks. One method is to cool the water to about 18 °C and then raise it about 2 °C a day.
A female can lay up to about 1,000 eggs. Remove the eggs early so the adults do not eat them, and use methylene blue to limit fungus.
During spawning season, males show white breeding tubercles on the gill covers and head.
Lays eggs. Breeding in an aquarium is not easy, and a separate tank set up to imitate spring may be needed.

health.fact: Prone to swim bladder disorders linked to the round body bred into it. The extreme shape may also harm the spine and organs and shorten its life.
Swim bladder trouble, bloating and constipation are common, mostly from overfeeding. The rounded body can bend the spine.
Gets sick more easily than ordinary goldfish. Common problems are digestive upsets, white spot, fin rot, bleeding and cloudy eyes.

buying.fact: Buy from reputable breeders or dealers. Before buying, watch the fish for signs of illness or trouble swimming.
Common in Vietnam, at about 25,000–50,000 VND each. Some lines cost more.
Colour may look pale after shipping. It usually comes back once the fish settles in.
Choose a bright, alert fish with strong colour that reaches into the fins.

controversy.fact: Some hobbyists and animal welfare advocates consider breeding goldfish for extreme body shapes cruel. Single-tailed goldfish such as comets have fewer health problems.
The care sheet raises ethical concerns about breeding for deformities and suggests single-tailed goldfish may be healthier and live longer.
